strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity characterization for CAMDPs—establishes minimax-optimal bounds for an important problem previously unexplored
Tight upper and lower bounds with respect to key parameters (S, A, B, H, ε) and clear separation between relaxed and strict feasibility regimes
Comprehensive technical analysis including non-trivial conversion from discounted to average-reward MDP concentration (Lemma 11) and careful error decomposition
Well-executed lower bound constructions via hard instances with occupancy measure separations and Fano's method
Clear presentation with well-motivated complexity parameters and proof sketches in main body
weaknesses: Restrictive assumptions limit practical applicability: generative model (simulator access) and known reward functions. No discussion of extensions to online learning or exploration settings

Limited algorithmic novelty: Algorithm 1 is straightforward adaptation of Vaswani et al. (2022) primal-dual method; main contribution is combining existing techniques rather than novel algorithmic insights
Zero experimental evaluation: no empirical validation, synthetic experiments, or computational complexity analysis. Constant factors in Õ notation could be large; practical utility is unclear
Dependence on problem-specific parameters (B, H, ζ) requires knowledge or estimation; severe 1/ζ² scaling for strict feasibility in nearly-infeasible problems is not discussed
No discussion of whether the 1/ζ² dependence for strict feasibility is fundamental or an artifact of the primal-dual approach; limited comparison with related settings

strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity characterization for CAMDPs in generative model setting, closing theoretical gap between constrained discounted MDPs and unconstrained average-reward MDPs
Complete theoretical analysis with matching upper bounds (relaxed and strict feasibility) and lower bounds via Fano's method, establishing minimax optimality

Technically sound proofs handling non-trivial challenges: connection between discounted and average-reward settings, careful concentration analysis, proper handling of Slater constant in dual optimization
Comprehensive treatment addressing both feasibility regimes with explicit algorithms and guarantees for each regime
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation: no experiments, simulations, or even toy examples demonstrating the bounds, despite this being expected for top-tier venues

Limited technical novelty: primal-dual algorithm directly adapts Vaswani et al. (2022), AMDP-to-discounted reduction is standard, lower bound closely follows Zurek & Chen (2024); main contribution is combining existing techniques rather than fundamental innovation

Critical finding insufficiently explained: the 1/ζ² dependence in strict feasibility (factor of ζ in Slater constant) is arguably the most important result but receives no intuitive explanation for why this dependence is fundamental or how to interpret it when ζ is small

Algorithm requires multiple problem-dependent parameters (ζ, B, H) with unclear estimation procedures: authors mention ζ 'can be estimated' without details; no robustness analysis for misspecification of B, H, or ζ

Highly restrictive model assumptions severely limit practical relevance: generative model only (no online RL), requires known reward/constraint functions, bounded transient time property, and weakly communicating/multichain MDPs only

Dense technical presentation lacking intuition: what does span bound H represent geometrically? Why does strict feasibility incur 1/ζ² cost? No worked examples or concrete instantiation for motivating wireless sensor network application
Polylogarithmic factors hidden in Õ notation obscure actual sample complexity; no discussion of whether bounds are practically achievable or merely theoretical existence results
Missing computational complexity analysis, robustness guarantees, and comparison with simpler approximations or online constrained RL approaches

Tight theoretical characterization with matching upper and lower bounds across key parameters (S, A, B, H, ζ, ε); establishes provable separation between relaxed and strict feasibility
Technically sound analysis: careful handling of AMDP-specific challenges (non-contractive Bellman), proper error decomposition, and rigorous information-theoretic lower bounds
Comprehensive treatment with both weakly communicating and general multichain MDPs, covering two practical feasibility regimes
Well-executed primal-dual algorithm design with detailed parameter selection and black-box AMDP solver integration
Extensive and rigorous proofs; complete algorithmic description supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited practical applicability: restricts to generative model setting (no online learning), assumes known rewards and constraints, no empirical validation or experiments
Heavy reliance on prior techniques (Vaswani et al. 2022, Zurek & Chen 2024); main novelty lies in careful combination for average-reward setting rather than new algorithmic ideas
ζ² factor in strict feasibility can be prohibitive when feasible region is small; constants hidden in Õ notation are not explicitly optimized
Algorithm 1 requires knowledge of ζ and has ~10 jointly-dependent parameters; parameter selection process (Sections 4-5) is intricate and not intuitive
Presentation is dense with heavy notation; could benefit from running examples, clearer intuition about parameter relationships, and simplified algorithm description
No discussion of extensions to function approximation, multiple constraints, or potential generalization to model-free settings; limited comparison to online constrained RL methods

strengths: First complete characterization of sample complexity for constrained average-reward MDPs, closing a gap in the literature
Near-optimal bounds with matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors, demonstrating the necessity of the ζ⁻² dependence for strict feasibility
Novel cross-signal concentration technique (Theorem 2) using reward perturbation and state-action absorbing construction to avoid uniform concentration over policy class
Rigorous technical analysis carefully managing transfer of guarantees from discounted to average-reward settings with well-designed bridge inequalities
Two complementary hard families that establish independent lower bounds for transient time and bias span regimes, combining to match the upper bound
Clear separation and provable gap between relaxed and strict feasibility regimes
Well-structured proof with careful attention to instance-dependent variance terms through conditional Bernstein hierarchy
weaknesses: Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance) is strong and lacks intuitive explanation; no examples of MDPs violating this condition are provided, limiting understanding of its necessity and applicability
Generative model assumption is restrictive and unrealistic; requires arbitrary state-action pair queries without exploration, limiting practical applicability

Algorithm is relatively standard (primal-dual with gradient descent on dual); most novelty is in analysis rather than algorithmic innovation; heavy reliance on prior work (Vaswani et al. 2022, Zurek & Chen 2024)
Strong dependence on unknown structural parameters (B, H, ζ); no discussion of sensitivity to misspecification or practical estimation of these parameters, particularly the Slater margin ζ
Notation-dense presentation makes the paper difficult to follow; key insights (algorithm intuition, average-to-discounted bridge) could appear much earlier with clearer exposition
No empirical validation or experiments; Õ notation hides polylog factors preventing finite-sample insights
Hard family constructions (6-state components, routing trees) are somewhat artificial and tailored to the proof; unclear connection to sample complexity in practical MDPs
Limited discussion of extensions (online setting, multi-constraint problems, computational complexity) and when techniques apply beyond average-reward setting

strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity characterization for constrained average-reward MDPs, filling a gap between prior work on unconstrained AMDPs and discounted CMDPs

Matching upper and lower bounds showing the strict-feasibility rate is minimax optimal (up to logarithmic factors); two independent hard families elegantly establish both H-scale and B-scale requirements
Clear separation between relaxed and strict feasibility regimes, with formal proof that ζ⁻² dependence is unavoidable for the latter but not the former

Technically sophisticated concentration result (Theorem 2: cross-signal concentration for Lagrangian oracle policies) avoiding uniform concentration over exponential policy classes via row-decoupling construction
Well-organized presentation with clear proof sketches in main text and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance condition) is neither well-justified nor systematically characterized—verified only on specific hard families; unclear when it holds on natural problems or if simpler conditions suffice

Zero empirical validation: no experiments, simulations, or algorithm implementations validating the bounds or demonstrating practical feasibility; opaque hidden constants in Õ notation make real-world implications unclear

Restricted to generative/simulator model setting, severely limiting practical applicability; unclear if sample complexity bounds reflect fundamental limits or artifacts of this model; online learning setting not addressed

Key concentration result (Theorem 2) obscures polylog factors: dependence on grid size |Λ|=O(ε⁻⁴), candidate set K, and hierarchy depth L=log(e/(1-γ)) create large hidden factors; practical scaling unclear

Proof techniques are largely incremental combinations of prior work (perturbed discounted MDPs from Vaswani et al. 2022, bridge lemmas from Zurek & Chen 2024); novelty primarily in formulation rather than methodology

Lower bound constructions (Sections 6-7, Appendices F-G) are ~20 pages of dense technical proofs lacking clear intuition for why instances are hard; difficult to verify and provide no conceptual insights
Algorithm 1 requires exact knowledge of problem-dependent constants (B, H, ζ) and brittle parameter tuning (e.g., γ=ε/(16(B+H))); no robustness analysis or adaptive parameter selection

Missing ablations and practical guidance: no analysis of problem-regime dependence, sensitivity to parameter misspecification, computational complexity, or when relaxed vs. strict feasibility should be preferred

strengths: First near-optimal sample complexity bounds for CAMDPs in average-reward setting with generative model access, solving an important open problem
Comprehensive theoretical results: matching upper bounds Õ(SA(B+H)/ε²) and Õ(SA(B+H)/(ε²ζ²)) with matching lower bounds up to logs for both relaxed and strict feasibility

Novel and sophisticated cross-signal concentration theorem (Theorem 2) that avoids uniform concentration over entire policy classes by controlling only finite families of Lagrangian oracle policies using reward perturbation and state-action absorbing construction

Clever hardness constructions: separate weakly communicating (span-dominated) and transient hard families that combine to achieve matching (B+H) lower bound, demonstrating both dependencies are necessary
Rigorous error decompositions distinguishing bridge, estimation, optimization, perturbation, and sensitivity errors with careful analysis of how each contributes to sample complexity
Proves fundamental separation between relaxed and strict feasibility regimes: ζ⁻² dependence for strict feasibility is shown to be unavoidable via matching lower bounds
weaknesses: Assumption 1 (policy-wise discounted variance condition) is non-trivial and restrictive; while verified for constructed hard families, limited guidance provided on when it holds for general MDPs, potentially limiting applicability

Results restricted to external mixtures of stationary deterministic policies; lack of discussion on why internal randomization or stochastic policies are insufficient and whether this is a fundamental barrier
Parameter choices in Algorithm 1 (e.g., 1-γ = ε/(16(B+H)), ω = ε/16) appear somewhat arbitrary; limited intuition for why these specific scalings are necessary, only that analysis justifies them
Polylog factors hide dependence on multiple parameters (δ, ε, ζ, ω, 1-γ, |Λ|, U, B+H); unclear which dependencies are fundamental vs. artifacts of proof technique

Dense technical presentation: key algorithmic ideas and motivation for perturbed empirical discounted MDPs could be explained more intuitively before detailed proofs; connection between the algorithmic approach and average-reward analysis deserves clearer exposition
No experimental validation, even synthetic experiments confirming scaling in key parameters (S, A, B, H, ζ) would strengthen claims about practical relevance
Strong generative model assumption limits applicability; no discussion of computational aspects or comparison to online learning sample complexity lower bounds
